answer: The control is ensure_ascii. DefaultJSONProvider sets it to True (src/flask/json/provider.py, around lines 166-179) before it calls json.dumps. With it on, every non-ASCII character in a serialized string, such as an accented letter, a CJK character or an emoji, is written as a unicode escape sequence, so the whole output is pure ASCII and safe in HTML and in any transport. The escape is lossless: json.loads turns it back into the original characters. A subclass that sets ensure_ascii to False keeps the characters as UTF-8 text, which is smaller and more readable but needs correct encoding downstream. The provider's response method still ends output with a newline and sets the mimetype. Because the flag lives on the provider, it applies uniformly to jsonify, dict and list return values, get_json and the tojson filter.

The flag is a per-object marker set on a Blueprint once app.register_blueprint has processed it (sansio/blueprints.py, around lines 316-321, where the blueprint is stored and marked registered). Blueprint setup methods are wrapped in setupmethod, which checks the flag and raises AssertionError if it is set. The reason is that a blueprint replays its recorded deferred functions at each registration. A route or hook added after the first registration would be missed by the apps already registered, or applied inconsistently to later registrations, and nothing would warn the developer. Failing loudly keeps the recorded state fixed once it has been copied onto an app. It is the blueprint-level analogue of the app's _got_first_request check, which is set at the first request rather than at registration.

Static serving is a blueprint feature layered on the same registration machinery. A Blueprint with a static_folder gets a static route added during register_blueprint (sansio/blueprints.py, step three of registration). The I/O half, src/flask/blueprints.py, defines send_static_file and get_send_file_max_age for the blueprint, and Flask in src/flask/app.py has the same two methods, with a note in blueprints.py (lines 55-65) saying they are duplicated. Caching stays consistent because both copies resolve the max age the same way: from SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT in config, unless a per-scope value overrides it, and the file is sent through the same send_file helper. So whether the app or a blueprint serves a file, the Cache-Control max-age follows the same rule. Changing one copy means changing the other.

The class is UnexpectedUnicodeError in src/flask/debughelpers.py. It is only useful in debug mode, where Flask explains likely mistakes instead of failing quietly. Its two bases express two layers of the problem. UnicodeError says the failure is an encoding problem, so existing code that catches decoding errors still recognizes it. AssertionError marks it as a developer-facing check of an assumption about the input, the kind of failure that signals a bug in how the app treats the data rather than bad user input. Together they separate the encoding fact from the programming-mistake interpretation. HTTP handling stays separate: the request still gets the normal response path, and production behavior is unchanged because debughelpers is only active when debug is on. I am not fully certain of the exact call site, so treat the trigger as a best reading.

The test (in tests/test_basic.py, a subdomain routing test) depends on a fixed chain. First, app.config SERVER_NAME is set, because subdomain matching needs a known server name to split the host into subdomain and base parts. Second, a route is registered with a subdomain, which becomes a Werkzeug Rule carrying that subdomain inside the app's url_map. Third, a request is created with a host that includes the subdomain, either through the test client or app.test_request_context with a base URL. RequestContext construction calls create_url_adapter, which binds the Map to that host using SERVER_NAME and the subdomain setting. Finally, match() selects the rule whose subdomain matches the request host. Each link depends on the one before it, so a missing SERVER_NAME breaks the whole chain at the adapter step.

Two mechanisms make the registered functions visible to rendering. The first is the shared Jinja environment: filters and globals registered through a blueprint's app-level decorators go through record_once and end up in app.jinja_env.filters, so they exist before any render, and every template in the app sees them. The second is the context processors. A blueprint's template_context_processor is recorded under the blueprint name in template_context_processors and merged into the app at registration (_merge_blueprint_funcs). At render time, render_template calls app.update_template_context, which runs the None-scope processors and then the processors for each scope in request.blueprints, outermost first. The results are merged into the one context dict that the shared environment renders. The only requirement is that the blueprint is registered and that the request belongs to it.

The helper class implements __fspath__, the protocol that os.fspath and path-aware standard library functions call to turn a path-like object into a string. When the standard library path conversion receives the object, it calls __fspath__ and expects a str or bytes result. The method returns the path string the test object wraps, unchanged, so the conversion yields a plain path that the open or os functions can use. Returning any other type would make the conversion raise TypeError. The test uses this to confirm that Flask's path handling accepts path-like objects and resolves them to the same file as a string would. I am giving the most likely behavior from the protocol, since the exact class body is not in the guide.

The parametrization supplies pairs of import names and app names. Some pairs name a module that cannot be imported, and others name a module that loads but has no matching attribute or factory. The test asserts that locate_app raises NoAppException in each case. The interaction is that both failure paths converge on one exception type. A failed import is caught and rewrapped as NoAppException with a message, and a missing name found by find_best_app raises the same exception. The CLI converts that exception into a clear Click error and exits, so users see one consistent failure instead of a raw ImportError or AttributeError. The parser runs before lookup, so the same behavior applies whether the argument is a plain name or a factory call. The function lives in src/flask/cli.py and the test in tests/test_cli.py.

The chain runs from the CLI helper, to the app, to the runner. A test provides an app to ScriptInfo, usually through the create_app callable, which is the first branch ScriptInfo.load_app checks before import-path discovery. The app then supplies app.cli, the AppGroup that holds its commands. FlaskCliRunner in src/flask/testing.py subclasses Click's CliRunner and passes the ScriptInfo object as obj when it invokes a command, so the loaded app is available to the command group. Click's runner isolates stdin, stdout and the exit code, so the command runs without a real process. The flask group then pushes an app context for app commands. Environment isolation comes from the autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py that resets FLASK_* variables around each test.

The chain is recursive dispatch. TagTuple.to_json calls serializer.tag on each element, and tag tries each registered tag in order until one matches. If an element is also a tuple, TagTuple matches again and recurses, so nested tuples are processed one level at a time down the structure. A true cycle needs a container that holds itself. Tuples are immutable, so a cycle must pass through a mutable container, usually a list or dict. Those are handled by PassList and PassDict, which call tag again on their items. A cycle such as a list containing a tuple that contains the same list would therefore recurse without bound until Python raises RecursionError. The tag pipeline has no cycle detection, and the session serializer assumes acyclic data. Plain nested tuples are safe because their depth is finite.

The test class separates the lifecycle of the request context from the behavior of the streamed response. A fixture or context-manager pattern owns the push and the matching pop, and it checks afterwards that no context is left pushed. The test methods then concentrate on what stream_with_context produces: they drive the generator and check the chunks and the values read from request inside it. This layering matches the leak_detector autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py, which pops and reports any context still pushed after a test. Keeping the lifecycle in one place means a failure in streaming logic does not hide a context leak, and the reverse. I am not certain of the exact class name, so this is the most likely architecture rather than a quoted detail.

The decorator is most likely after_this_request. It appends the function to the current request context's list of after-request callbacks. Its coupling is to whichever RequestContext is active at the moment of the call. Those callbacks run in process_response for that request, after the after_request functions, in the order they were registered. Nested calls simply add more callbacks, so the execution order depends on code path rather than on the decorator. Conditional registration works only if the view reaches the call before the response is finalized. A call made after the response is built, or outside a request context, raises RuntimeError or is never run. Because the state lives on the context and not on the decorated function, it does not leak between requests, but it does depend on the response lifecycle the decorator is attached to.

The wrapper defers the hashlib lookup from import time to call time. Some constructors, such as md5 or sha1, can be missing or can raise on platforms where the digest is restricted, for example in FIPS-enabled Python builds. If the module evaluated them at import, the whole package would fail before any application code ran. By wrapping the access in a function, the module imports cleanly, and the error appears only when a digest is actually needed, such as signing a session cookie. The behavior is predictable: import never fails for this reason, and use fails at the point where the algorithm matters. The session signing path uses SHA-1 through the serializer's digest method, so the deferred call is what matters there. I am giving the most likely purpose; the exact helper name and location are not quoted in the guide.

copy_current_request_context captures the active request context when the decorator is applied. When the wrapped function runs in a greenlet, it calls the captured context's copy method, which builds a new RequestContext with the same app, the same Request object, the same URL adapter and the same session object. It then pushes that copy inside the new greenlet, runs the function and pops the copy. Because the session is shared by reference, reads and writes in the copy are visible to the original request, so session data is preserved across the boundary. Isolation comes from ContextVar semantics: the push sets the variable only in the greenlet's own context, so the copy does not disturb the original context's state. The guide notes that this decorator exists for greenlets (src/flask/ctx.py, around lines 155-193), because ContextVar values are not inherited automatically.

CertParamType.convert in src/flask/cli.py tries the value in order and returns on the first success. If the value names an existing file, it returns that path so the certificate is loaded from disk, with the key option supplied separately. If the value is the literal adhoc, it returns that marker so Werkzeug generates a temporary self-signed certificate. If it is an import string of the form module:name, it imports the object and expects it to be an SSLContext. Anything else fails through Click's error mechanism with a message. The option is used only by flask run --cert, and the file-path check comes first, so a real file always wins over an import path of the same form. I am not certain of the exact order of the last two branches, so treat that part as the most likely reading.

The app-level template filter decorator on a blueprint does not register immediately. It calls record_once, so the blueprint stores a deferred function that runs when the blueprint is registered. That function calls the app's add_template_filter, which writes into app.jinja_env.filters. Filters are keyed by name, not by URL, so the url_prefix passed to register_blueprint has no effect on whether the filter exists. The prefix only changes the routes built by BlueprintSetupState. Because the filter lands in the one Jinja environment for the app, any template rendered by any view, including app-level templates, can use it. Registering the blueprint twice under different names does not duplicate the filter, because record_once applies the deferred function only once. That is why hooks and filters ignore the URL prefix while routes respect it.

TagBytes.to_json calls base64.b64encode on the bytes and decodes the result to ASCII text, so the stored value is plain JSON text. For example, b"x" becomes the text eA== inside a one-key dict whose key is a space followed by b. to_python reverses this with base64.b64decode, which returns exactly the original byte string. Base64 is a bijection between byte strings and its alphabet, and the padding is included, so decoding always recovers the same bytes. The alphabet contains only letters, digits, plus, slash and equals, so the text survives JSON and cookie encoding without escaping. The session signature from ItsDangerous covers the encoded text, so any tampering with the base64 is rejected before decoding. Binary data round-trips exactly through this path.

handle_exception (src/flask/app.py, around lines 811-862) decides after it has logged the event. First it sends the got_request_exception signal. Then, if PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS is true, it re-raises the original exception so the server or test sees the traceback. If the setting is None, its default, it propagates only while app.testing or app.debug is on. Otherwise it logs the error through the app logger, builds an InternalServerError with original_exception set, and finalizes it into a 500 response, passing it to a registered 500 handler if there is one. So the decision is driven by configuration: an explicit PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS overrides everything, a None value follows testing or debug mode, and in production the caller gets a 500 response. The method is reached from wsgi_app when an exception escapes full_dispatch_request.

Blueprint.add_url_rule checks the endpoint name for dots and then appends a lambda to deferred_functions. When the lambda is called with a BlueprintSetupState, it calls that state's add_url_rule with the captured rule, view function and options. The deferral is needed because a blueprint does not know its app, its final URL prefix, its subdomain or its name prefix. Those are decided only at register_blueprint time, and one blueprint may be registered several times under different prefixes or names. Storing the replayable call keeps the blueprint reusable: each registration replays the same recorded rules with its own state, which joins the prefix and prefixes the endpoint with the registered name. Once a blueprint has been registered, its setup methods raise, so the list cannot change under a live app. This is the design in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py.

The session is a CallbackDict whose update callback sets the modified and accessed flags on every write. The app writes the cookie only when the flag is set, so the in-memory dict and the persisted cookie agree at the end of each request. Each request gets its own session object, built from the cookie that request sent, so concurrent requests do not share mutable session state inside one process. The trade-off is across requests from the same browser. Two concurrent requests can each write a full session, and the response that arrives last overwrites the cookie, discarding the other request's change. Flask does not lock or merge session changes between requests. Nested mutation is not tracked, so developers must set modified manually, which keeps the top-level write path simple and predictable.

The namespace is _AppCtxGlobals, one instance per AppContext, created in AppContext.__init__ and exposed as g (src/flask/ctx.py, around lines 245-254). It is not a process global. The AppContext is stored in the ContextVar _cv_app, and each thread or asyncio task has its own value of that variable. So g, reached through the proxy, resolves to the active context only in the current thread or task. Two concurrent requests in different threads each push their own app context and therefore see separate g objects. Within a single context the object is a plain attribute store with no lock, so threads started from a view that share the same g are not protected and need their own synchronization. Isolation comes from the context boundary, not from locking.

The class uses two conventions on purpose. Attribute access through __getattr__ raises AttributeError for a missing name, which is what Python expects, so hasattr and getattr with a default behave normally. Deletion through __delattr__ also raises AttributeError when the name is absent. The dictionary-style methods instead take defaults. get returns a supplied default when the key is missing, pop with a default returns that value rather than raising, and setdefault stores a default if the key is absent. So attribute access stays strict and matches object semantics, while the explicit methods offer a non-raising path. Code that wants a fallback should use g.get or g.pop with a default. The guide lists get, pop, setdefault and membership as the supported surface, and this split is how the class balances strictness with convenience.

The annotation is the ResponseReturnValue family in src/flask/typing.py, a union alias. It accepts strings, bytes, dicts, lists, iterators, Response objects, WSGI callables and tuples that add a status and headers. A dict in that union is typed as a mapping, not as JSON, so the annotation describes only the shape the type checker may see at the return site. The serialization happens later, in make_response, which hands dicts and lists to the app's JSON provider. Status and headers are kept separate by the tuple forms, so the status code is not part of the body type. This decouples the payload from HTTP status: the view types its body, and the tuple form carries the code and headers. The alias is a static-typing device with no runtime effect on how the response is built.

MethodView.__init_subclass__ (src/flask/views.py, around lines 165-180) builds the methods set for each subclass. It starts with the HTTP verb functions the class defines, such as get, post and delete, and then merges in the methods attribute of any base class that has one. The conflict rule is union, not override: a verb is allowed if any class in the hierarchy defines it. The result is stored as cls.methods, which the router reads when it creates rules. Which implementation actually runs is decided separately, by ordinary Python method resolution on the instance during dispatch_request. So the set controls which verbs are routed, and the method resolution order controls which function answers each verb. Keeping the two concerns apart is why multiple inheritance of view classes behaves predictably.

TagUUID exists because JSON has no UUID type, and a UUID must come back as a UUID object rather than a string. to_json returns value.hex, a 32-character hexadecimal string with no hyphens, which is compact enough for a cookie. to_python returns uuid.UUID built from that string, and the result compares equal to the original. The round trip is exact because the hex form is canonical and loses nothing. Bidirectional conversion matters because the session serializer untags values on load. If only the encoding direction existed, a session would return a plain string, and comparisons with UUID objects would fail silently. The tag key with the leading space keeps the value distinct from user data. TagDateTime and TagBytes follow the same two-way pattern.

The async method view inherits from the synchronous dispatch base because the dispatch logic is identical in both cases. Dispatch finds the method for request.method, falls back from HEAD to GET where appropriate, and calls it with the URL arguments. The only difference is that a handler may be a coroutine function. Flask wraps views with ensure_sync, including in views.py around line 110, so when a method is async it is wrapped with async_to_sync and the same dispatch code works without change. Duplicating dispatch would copy the verb lookup, the HEAD fallback and the method merging, and the copies would drift apart over time. Inheritance keeps one routing path and one place for changes, while the async behavior lives in the ensure_sync wrapper. This is consistent with Flask's design of a synchronous core with async added as a wrapper around user code.

ScriptInfo takes two alternatives because two kinds of caller hold different information. The command line only has a string, the import path, and needs lazy resolution from it. Programmatic callers such as tests, custom FlaskGroup subclasses and embedding code already hold a factory, which is the create_app callable, and should not go through discovery. ScriptInfo.load_app checks create_app first. If it is set, it calls it; otherwise it resolves the import path through the discovery functions. This gives the command group one object to carry, regardless of where the app comes from. The two parameters are alternatives in practice: whichever is supplied decides the path. The design keeps the test runner and the command-line entry point on the same code path after the app is obtained.

open_resource is meant for reading packaged data such as templates, static files or other resources that ship with the application. Restricting it to read-only modes such as r, rt, rb and their variants keeps it from writing into the package or the root directory. An installed package is usually read-only, and its resources should not change at runtime. Data the application writes belongs in the instance folder or another configured location. The restriction also protects against accidental truncation, since a write mode passed by mistake would otherwise erase a file. Invalid modes raise ValueError rather than opening silently. The check validates only the mode argument, and the method otherwise stays a simple reader that resolves paths relative to root_path in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py.

Discovery is deferred because it is slow and can fail. Importing the user's module can run side effects, read configuration and build the app. Lazy loading means flask --help, version output and listing commands never import the application, which keeps them fast and lets them work even when the app is broken. The loaded app is stored in the _loaded_app attribute, so the first command that needs it loads it and later calls in the same process reuse the object, avoiding repeated factory calls. The ordering also matters for options. The group's --debug and --env-file options write environment variables before any import happens, and that only works if loading happens after option parsing. Initialization therefore stores just the import path or factory, and load_app does the real work when a command asks for the app.

Each read method sets accessed to True, which is a plain attribute write on the session object and is cheap in itself. The cost comes from what the flag causes later. Once accessed is true, the save step adds a Vary: Cookie header to the response, so caches are told the response depends on the cookie, and the save decision runs for every request that read the session. Frequent reads therefore add header work and keep the save path active on each response. Serialization and signing happen only when the session is modified, or when a permanent session is due for refresh, so reads alone do not re-sign the cookie. The unconditional marking is therefore a small per-read overhead plus a response-level effect rather than a serialization cost. This reading follows the session section of the guide, though the exact measured impact is not documented there.

Each call to a blueprint's app-level template filter decorator records a deferred function. If the same filter is repeated across many blueprint objects, each blueprint carries its own deferred list, and at registration each one is replayed against the app. record_once ensures a given callback applies only once per app, and the filter is then stored by name in the Jinja environment's filters dict. The total work grows with the number of blueprints times the number of repeated decorator calls, which is linear and happens only at startup. Performance would degrade noticeably only if registration were repeated per request or nested in a loop that re-runs the setup. Repeated filter entries overwrite the same name rather than accumulating. At request time nothing is slower, because filters are looked up by name in a dict. The concern is startup overhead, not request latency.

Blueprint names become the leading part of endpoint names, and Flask finds a request's blueprint by splitting the endpoint on its last dot (request.blueprint). A dot inside a blueprint name would make that split ambiguous. An endpoint like a.b.view could mean blueprint a.b with view, or nested blueprint b inside a. So the Blueprint constructor in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py raises ValueError when the name contains a dot, and the test checks that creating a blueprint with such a name, or adding a route to it, raises that error. The test guards the invariant that endpoint dots mark exactly one boundary. Nested blueprints still work because the parent name is joined with a dot internally through name_prefix, and the user never supplies the dot. The check prevents silently wrong hook scoping and url_for resolution.

The session persistence handler builds a URLSafeTimedSerializer through get_signing_serializer each time it is needed, both when opening a session and when saving one. Building the serializer creates a new object and derives a signing key from the secret key and the salt, using HMAC with SHA-1. Because this runs once or twice per request and is not cached, the same key derivation repeats for every request. Under high concurrency that adds CPU work on every worker, and the cost multiplies with request volume. The cost is small for each call, but it is never amortized. Caching the serializer per app, or per key list, would remove most of the repeated work, but it would need to handle configuration changes at runtime. The guide documents the key list and salt construction in src/flask/sessions.py.

PassDict tags only values because JSON object keys are always strings. A key cannot hold a tuple, bytes or another tagged type, so the only place a non-JSON value can appear in a dict is its value. Tagging keys would also be impossible in plain JSON, since keys must be strings. Keeping keys untouched means the dict's keys come back exactly as they went in when the untag scan runs after parsing. The one-key tag dicts are recognized by their key, and that recognition applies to the shape of a dict, so rewriting user keys could let them collide with tag names. The design is minimal: tag what can hold a value, and leave keys alone. The recursion goes through the values because they are the only place where nested tagged structures can occur.

The test adds a stream handler to the root logger and then checks that app.logger.handlers is empty. Flask's logger setup in src/flask/logging.py adds its default handler only when no existing handler can already handle the logger's effective level. It checks this with a level-handler test that walks up the logger hierarchy to the root. If the root logger already has a stream handler, the app logger is covered, so Flask adds nothing and records propagate to the root handler and print once. The empty list is the expected result, showing that Flask did not attach a duplicate. The test guards the design rule that the application's logging configuration wins over Flask's default and that messages are not printed twice.

The transformation happens in make_config, in the sans-IO App class (src/flask/sansio/app.py, around lines 482-496). When instance_relative_config is true, the root path used for the config object is replaced by the instance path, which comes from the app's instance_path. That replacement happens before the config object is created. The Config constructor then stores this root path, and relative file loaders such as from_pyfile resolve against it. make_config also copies the default configuration, sets DEBUG from FLASK_DEBUG, and creates config_class(root_path, defaults) in that same step. So editing how instance-relative configuration behaves means changing make_config, not the loaders.

The control flow is in FlaskGroup.get_command (src/flask/cli.py, around lines 609-634). First it checks the group's own registered commands for a directly added command, which covers built-ins such as run, shell and routes. If that fails, it looks for plugin commands discovered through the flask.commands entry point group, which are loaded without importing the application. Only if both fail does it consult the application: it calls ScriptInfo.load_app and, if the app has a CLI group, returns the command from app.cli, pushing an app context first so current_app is available. The order means built-in commands take precedence over plugins, plugins over application commands, and the application is imported only when a command actually needs it.

TagMarkup delegates to protocol methods and constructors from MarkupSafe. For serialization, to_json calls the value's __html__ method, which returns the raw HTML text of a Markup object. For deserialization, to_python wraps the stored string back in markupsafe.Markup, which marks it as already safe. Markup is a str subclass defined in the MarkupSafe package, so its trust semantics and escaping rules come from there. The __html__ protocol is the same one Flask's JSON provider recognizes for objects with HTML, so the two parts of the code agree on how safe HTML is represented. The lower-level helpers are therefore the __html__ method on the value and the Markup constructor, both imported in src/flask/json/tag.py.

PassList.to_json maps each item through serializer.tag, which is the central type dispatcher. The dispatcher walks the registered tags in their fixed order, and asks each one whether it applies. The first match converts the item. A nested list matches PassList again and recurses. A tuple matches TagTuple. A dict matches PassDict or TagDict, and scalars pass through unchanged. Mixed nested structures are handled one element at a time, with the same ordering rule at every level. The recursion ends at scalars, which PassList leaves alone. On load, the untag scan works in the reverse direction, bottom-up, decoding nested values before their parents. So the list tag is a thin loop over a shared dispatcher rather than a separate serialization rule.

The decision is made in App.add_url_rule (src/flask/sansio/app.py, around lines 604-661). The provide_automatic_options argument is consulted first. If it is None, Flask reads the view function's provide_automatic_options attribute, and if that is also unset, it decides from the PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS config key together with whether OPTIONS is already among the methods. If the automatic flag is on, OPTIONS is added to the rule's methods. At dispatch time, in Flask.dispatch_request (src/flask/app.py, around lines 879-902), a request with method OPTIONS on a rule that has the flag set receives the automatic answer from make_default_options_response, and the view is not called. So registration decides both the flag and the method set, and dispatch acts on the flag.

The lookup is in App._find_error_handler (src/flask/sansio/app.py, around lines 823-846). It builds the candidate scopes from the request: the blueprint names in request.blueprints, followed by None for the app. The guide describes the sequence as the blueprint handler for the status code, then the app handler for the code, then the blueprint handler for the exception class, then the app handler for the class. For classes it walks the exception's method resolution order, so a handler for a base class catches subclasses that have no more specific handler. The status code check happens before any class check, so a code-specific handler at app level beats a class handler at blueprint level. The lookup returns the first match and stops.

The test class that validates URL generation with anchors, schemes and HTTP methods is most likely in tests/test_helpers.py, alongside the other helper tests, under a class about url_for. The keywords it exercises are the url_for options _anchor for fragments, _scheme for the scheme and _external for absolute URLs, and _method, which selects the rule that accepts a given HTTP method. The guide does not quote the class name, so I am giving the likely location rather than a verified one. If the class is not in that file, the next place to look is tests/test_basic.py, which holds the largest set of routing and URL tests.

The encoding argument flows from the test into the file-opening step. The test calls the resource-opening method on the app or on a blueprint with an encoding, and checks that the file is read with that encoding. The method lives in src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py, where the resource path is joined to root_path and then passed to the built-in open call with the mode and the encoding. The app and blueprint versions differ in their default: the app uses the locale default, while the blueprint uses UTF-8, as the guide notes. The test therefore confirms that an explicit encoding reaches the open call rather than being ignored. The mode check runs before the file is opened, so write modes are rejected first. I am giving the most likely path of the argument, since the exact signature is not quoted in the guide.

TagBytes.to_python calls base64.b64decode. It runs during the untag step of TaggedJSONSerializer, after json.loads has parsed the cookie text. The untag function, _untag_scan in src/flask/json/tag.py (around lines 297-319), walks the parsed structure bottom-up. When it finds a one-key dict whose key is the bytes tag, a space followed by b, it passes the value to that tag's to_python. Nested values are decoded before their parents, so the base64 decode sees plain strings. ItsDangerous has already checked the signature inside loads before any of this runs, so tampered data never reaches the decoder. The decode is therefore the last conversion step in reading a session value back.

Config.from_object accepts an object, which can be a class. It iterates the names returned by dir on that object, and dir includes attributes inherited from base classes. A configuration subclass therefore picks up uppercase settings from its parents automatically. A value defined in the subclass overrides the parent's value of the same name, because attribute lookup on the class follows the method resolution order. Only uppercase names are copied, so helper methods and lowercase attributes are skipped. This means configuration class inheritance behaves like ordinary Python. A common pattern is a base Config class with DevelopmentConfig and ProductionConfig subclasses, and app.config.from_object(ProductionConfig) then gets the full resolved set. The loader is in src/flask/config.py.

The orchestration sits in the request pipeline. The session is loaded in RequestContext.push (src/flask/ctx.py, around lines 384-389), which happens inside wsgi_app before any view runs. It is saved in process_response (src/flask/app.py, around lines 1321-1322), which finalize_request calls after the view, the error handlers and the after_request functions have run. The two steps share no lock. Each request has its own session object, built from its own cookie, so there is no shared mutable state to race on inside one process. Across concurrent requests from the same browser, the result is last writer wins on the cookie, with no merge. Within one request the steps are sequential, and between requests they are independent. The race risk is therefore client-side, not inside the server's session code.

The route handler that returns a list of dictionaries sits in a file under tests/type_check, a directory that exists only to be type-checked. Flask's route decorator is typed with the ResponseReturnValue alias in src/flask/typing.py, and a function returning a list of dictionaries is checked against that alias because list is one of its members. The pyproject.toml configuration for mypy and pyright includes tests/type_check in its strict checks, so the annotation has to be accepted or the typing job fails. The checks run as part of the tox typing environment. Reveal-type or assert-type lines in the file confirm the inferred type. I am not certain of the exact file name, but this is the mechanism the configuration sets up.

_find_error_handler walks the exception's method resolution order with a Python loop. For each class in the chain it performs up to four dictionary lookups, across the blueprint and app scopes and the code and class keys. The cost is therefore proportional to the depth of the class hierarchy times the number of scopes, and each step is an O(1) dictionary lookup. The walk stops at the first registered match, so a handler close to the exception class is found quickly. An exception that matches nothing walks the whole chain before falling through. For typical hierarchies of five to ten classes this is a handful of lookups per error, which is negligible next to building the error response. There is no cache, so repeated errors repeat the walk. Optimizing would mean caching the result per exception class and scope.
